title: Network Delay Time
description:
You are given a network of `n` nodes labeled from `1` to `n`. You are also given `times`, a list of directed travel times as triples `times[i] = [u_i, v_i, w_i]`, where `u_i` is the source node, `v_i` is the target node, and `w_i` is the time it takes for a signal to travel from `u_i` to `v_i`.

We send a signal from a given node `k`. Return the **minimum time** it takes for all `n` nodes to receive the signal. If it is impossible for all `n` nodes to receive the signal, return `-1`.
constraints: All pairs (u_i, v_i) are unique (no multiple directed edges between the same pair).
hints: All edge weights are non-negative, so the earliest time each node receives the signal is its shortest-path distance from node `k`.
Run Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap starting from `(0, k)` and relax outgoing edges from each popped node, skipping stale heap entries.
Once all reachable nodes are settled, return `-1` if fewer than `n` nodes were reached; otherwise return the maximum shortest-path distance across all `n` nodes.

examples.explanation: From node 2, the signal reaches nodes 1 and 3 at time 1, and reaches node 4 via 2 -> 3 -> 4 at time 2. All 4 nodes receive the signal by time 2.
The signal travels directly from node 1 to node 2 in 1 unit of time.
The only edge goes from 1 to 2, so starting at node 2 can never reach node 1.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
description:
There are `n` cities connected by some number of directed flights. You are given an array `flights` where `flights[i] = [from_i, to_i, price_i]` indicates that there is a flight from city `from_i` to city `to_i` with cost `price_i`.

You are also given three integers `src`, `dst`, and `k`. Return the **cheapest price** from `src` to `dst` with **at most `k` stops** (intermediate cities, meaning at most `k + 1` flights). If there is no such route, return `-1`.
constraints: There are no multiple flights between the same pair (from_i, to_i).
hints: At most `k` stops means a path can use at most `k + 1` directed edges.
Run `k + 1` rounds of Bellman-Ford edge relaxation. In each round, read distances from the previous round's snapshot so a single round adds at most one edge to any path.
If you use Dijkstra's algorithm instead, be careful not to discard a more expensive path to a node if it uses fewer stops than previously seen paths to that node.

examples.explanation: With at most 1 stop, the path 0 -> 1 -> 3 costs 100 + 600 = 700. Although 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 costs 400, it uses 2 stops and is not allowed.
The optimal path with at most 1 stop is 0 -> 1 -> 2 with total cost 100 + 100 = 200, cheaper than the direct flight costing 500.
With 0 stops allowed, only the direct flight 0 -> 2 with cost 500 is valid.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
description:
You are a hiker preparing for an upcoming hike. You are given `heights`, a 2D array of size `rows x columns`, where `heights[row][col]` represents the height of cell `(row, col)`. You are situated in the top-left cell `(0, 0)`, and you hope to travel to the bottom-right cell `(rows - 1, columns - 1)` (0-indexed). You can move **up, down, left, or right**, and you wish to find a route that requires the minimum **effort**.

A route's **effort** is the **maximum absolute difference** in heights between two consecutive cells of the route.

Return the minimum **effort** required to travel from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell.
hints: Model the grid as an undirected weighted graph where the weight of an edge between two adjacent cells is `|heights[r1][c1] - heights[r2][c2]|`, and path cost is the maximum edge weight along the path rather than the sum.
Because the path cost `max(effortSoFar, edgeWeight)` is monotonically non-decreasing as edges are appended, Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap finds the exact minimum effort to every cell.
Alternatively, binary search on the allowed maximum effort `mid` in `[0, 10^6]` and check with BFS/DFS whether `(rows - 1, columns - 1)` is reachable using only transitions with difference `<= mid`.

examples.explanation: The route [1, 3, 5, 3, 5] has a maximum absolute difference of 2 in consecutive cells, which is better than [1, 2, 2, 2, 5] with a maximum difference of 3.
The route [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] has a maximum absolute difference of 1, which is optimal.
A winding route following the cells of height 1 connects the top-left to the bottom-right with effort 0.

title: Swim in Rising Water
description:
You are given an `n x n` integer matrix `grid` where each value `grid[i][j]` represents the elevation at cell `(i, j)`.

It starts raining, and at time `t`, the water level everywhere is `t`. You can swim from a cell to another 4-directionally adjacent cell if and only if the elevation of **both** cells is at most `t`. You can swim infinite distances in zero time, as long as you stay within the boundaries of the grid.

Return the **least time `t`** until you can reach the bottom-right cell `(n - 1, n - 1)` starting from the top-left cell `(0, 0)`.
hints: A path from `(0, 0)` to `(n - 1, n - 1)` is traversable at time `t` if and only if every cell on the path has elevation `<= t`. Thus we want to minimize the maximum cell elevation along the path.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap keyed by the elevation of each frontier cell (or `max(timeSoFar, grid[r][c])`), starting from `(grid[0][0], 0, 0)`.
Because elevations are unique integers in `[0, n^2 - 1]`, you can also binary search on `t` with BFS/DFS or use Union-Find ordered by cell elevation.

examples.explanation: At time 0 you are at (0, 0). You cannot enter (1, 1) until time 3, so the minimum time to reach the bottom-right corner is 3.
The optimal path winds around the right and bottom edges through elevations 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 16 -> 15 -> ... -> 6, whose maximum elevation is 16.
You start at (0, 0) with elevation 3, so even though the remaining cells have smaller elevations, you must wait until time 3 to move.

title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
description:
Given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid`, return the length of the shortest **clear path** in the matrix. If there is no clear path, return `-1`.

A **clear path** in a binary matrix is a path from the top-left cell `(0, 0)` to the bottom-right cell `(n - 1, n - 1)` such that:
- All visited cells of the path have value `0`.
- Every pair of consecutive visited cells is **8-directionally connected** (they are different and share an edge or a corner).

The **length** of a clear path is the number of visited cells along the path (including both the starting and ending cells).
hints: First check the boundary conditions: if `grid[0][0] == 1` or `grid[n - 1][n - 1] == 1`, no clear path can exist, so return `-1` immediately.

Because every valid step to any of the 8 neighbors has uniform weight `1`, Breadth-First Search (a unit-weight specialization of Dijkstra's algorithm) discovers `(n - 1, n - 1)` in the minimum number of cells.
Mark cells as visited when enqueuing them (not when dequeuing) to avoid pushing duplicates into the queue.

examples.explanation: Move diagonally from (0, 0) directly to (1, 1), visiting 2 cells.
The shortest clear path is (0, 0) -> (0, 1) -> (1, 2) -> (2, 2), which visits 4 cells.
The starting cell (0, 0) is blocked (1), so no clear path exists.

title: Shortest Path to Get All Keys
description:
You are given an `m x n` grid where each cell is represented by a character:
- `'.'` is an empty cell.
- `'#'` is a wall (impassable).
- `'@'` is the starting point.
- Lowercase English letters (`'a'` to `'f'`) represent **keys**.
- Uppercase English letters (`'A'` to `'F'`) represent **locks**.

You start at `'@'` and can move one cell up, down, left, or right per step. You cannot walk outside the grid or into a wall. Stepping onto a key collects it permanently. You cannot walk onto a lock unless you already hold its corresponding lowercase key.

There are `k` keys in the grid (`1 <= k <= 6`), using the first `k` lowercase letters, and each key has a matching lock. Return the **lowest number of moves** required to acquire all `k` keys. If it is impossible, return `-1`.
constraints: The number of keys k is in the range [1, 6].
Each key 'a' through chr('a' + k - 1) appears exactly once and has exactly one matching lock.
There is exactly one starting cell '@'.
hints: Because revisiting a cell is useful after acquiring a new key, your shortest-path state must include both your position and the set of collected keys.
Since there are at most `6` keys, represent the collected key set as a `k`-bit integer bitmask `(0 .. 2^k - 1)`.
Run Breadth-First Search over states `(row, col, keyMask)`. When stepping onto a key, set its bit in `keyMask`; stop as soon as `keyMask == (1 << k) - 1`.

examples.explanation: Move right to collect key 'a', go down through column 3, unlock 'A', and continue left to collect key 'b' in 8 moves total.
Walk right along row 0 to pick up 'a' and unlock 'A', then step down along column 4 to pick up 'b' in 6 moves.
Lock 'A' blocks the only path to key 'a', making it impossible to collect all keys.

title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
description: Given an undirected weighted graph, count for each city how many other cities are reachable with shortest-path distance at most `distanceThreshold`. Return the city with the fewest such neighbors; if there is a tie, return the city with the largest index.
hints: Represent the graph with adjacency lists or a distance matrix appropriate to the limits.
Track shortest-distance states and respect all time or threshold rules.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { public int findTheCity(int n,int[][] e,int t) { int inf=1000000000;int[][] d=new int[n][n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){Arrays.fill(d[i],inf);d[i][i]=0;}for(int[] x:e){d[x[0]][x[1]]=x[2];d[x[1]][x[0]]=x[2];}for(int k=0;k<n;k++)for(int i=0;i<n;i++)for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if(d[i][k]<inf&&d[k][j]<inf)d[i][j]=Math.min(d[i][j],d[i][k]+d[k][j]);int best=-1,min=Integer.MAX_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<n;i++){int c=0;for(int j=0;j<n;j++)if(i!=j&&d[i][j]<=t)c++;if(c<=min){min=c;best=i;}}return best;} }

title: Second Minimum Time to Reach Destination
description: An undirected connected graph has nodes 1 through `n`. Traversing any edge takes `time` minutes. At every node, the traffic signal alternates between green and red in intervals of `change` minutes; you may leave only when it is green, and you cannot wait voluntarily during green. Return the second distinct arrival time from node 1 to node n.
constraints: edges form a connected simple graph
hints: Represent the graph with adjacency lists or a distance matrix appropriate to the limits.
Track shortest-distance states and respect all time or threshold rules.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { public int secondMinimum(int n,int[][] e,int time,int change) { List<Integer>[] g=new List[n+1];for(int i=1;i<=n;i++)g[i]=new ArrayList<>();for(int[] x:e){g[x[0]].add(x[1]);g[x[1]].add(x[0]);}int[] a=new int[n+1],b=new int[n+1];Arrays.fill(a,-1);Arrays.fill(b,-1);ArrayDeque<int[]>q=new ArrayDeque<>();a[1]=0;q.add(new int[]{1,0});int steps=-1;while(!q.isEmpty()&&steps<0){int[] z=q.remove();for(int v:g[z[0]]){int d=z[1]+1;if(a[v]<0){a[v]=d;q.add(new int[]{v,d});}else if(b[v]<0&&d>a[v]){b[v]=d;if(v==n){steps=d;break;}q.add(new int[]{v,d});}}}int cur=0;for(int i=0;i<steps;i++){if((cur/change)%2==1)cur=((cur/change)+1)*change;cur+=time;}return cur;} }

title: Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time
description: An undirected edge `[u,v,t]` takes `t` minutes to traverse. Visiting node `i` incurs `passingFees[i]`. Starting at node 0 at time 0, return the minimum total fee to reach node `n-1` within `maxTime`; return -1 if impossible. Fees are paid once each time a node is visited.
hints: Represent the graph with adjacency lists or a distance matrix appropriate to the limits.
Track shortest-distance states and respect all time or threshold rules.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { public int minCost(int mt,int[][] e,int[] f) { int n=f.length;List<int[]>[] g=new List[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)g[i]=new ArrayList<>();for(int[] x:e){g[x[0]].add(new int[]{x[1],x[2]});g[x[1]].add(new int[]{x[0],x[2]});}int[][] d=new int[mt+1][n];for(int[] r:d)Arrays.fill(r,Integer.MAX_VALUE);d[0][0]=f[0];PriorityQueue<int[]>q=new PriorityQueue<>((a,b)->Integer.compare(a[0],b[0]));q.add(new int[]{f[0],0,0});while(!q.isEmpty()){int[] z=q.remove();int c=z[0],t=z[1],u=z[2];if(c!=d[t][u])continue;if(u==n-1)return c;for(int[] x:g[u]){int nt=t+x[1],nc=c+f[x[0]];if(nt<=mt&&nc<d[nt][x[0]]){d[nt][x[0]]=nc;q.add(new int[]{nc,nt,x[0]});}}}return -1;} }

title: Count Shortest Routes
description: An undirected connected graph has `n` vertices numbered 0 through `n-1`. Each road is `[u, v, time]` with positive travel time. Count the distinct shortest routes from vertex 0 to vertex `n-1`, modulo 1,000,000,007. Input: `n` and `roads`. Output: the route count.
constraints: The graph is connected and has no parallel roads
hints: Represent each edge as a transition whose cost matches the route rule.
Keep the best distance for each required state and ignore stale priority-queue entries.

title: Maximum Probability Path
description: An undirected graph has `n` vertices. Each edge `edges[i] = [u,v]` succeeds with probability `succProb[i]`. The probability of a path is the product of its edge probabilities. Return the maximum probability of reaching `end` from `start`, or 0 if no path exists. Input: `n`, `edges`, `succProb`, `start`, `end`. Output: the maximum probability.
hints: Represent each edge as a transition whose cost matches the route rule.
Keep the best distance for each required state and ignore stale priority-queue entries.

title: Shortest Route With One Discount
description: An undirected connected graph has `n` vertices and positive weighted edges `[u,v,cost]`. Travel costs `cost`, except that you may choose at most one edge on your route and pay `floor(cost/2)` for it. Return the minimum possible cost from `source` to `destination`. Input: `n`, `edges`, `source`, `destination`. Output: the minimum cost.
constraints: The graph is connected and has no parallel edges
hints: Represent each edge as a transition whose cost matches the route rule.
Keep the best distance for each required state and ignore stale priority-queue entries.

title: Bellman-Ford Distance List
description: A directed weighted graph has vertices `0..n-1` and edges `[u,v,w]`; edge weights may be negative. There are no negative-weight cycles reachable from `source`. Return the shortest distance from `source` to every vertex, using -1 for unreachable vertices. Input: `n`, `edges`, `source`. Output: a distance array.
constraints: No negative cycle is reachable from source; all shortest distances fit in signed 32-bit range
hints: Represent each edge as a transition whose cost matches the route rule.
Keep the best distance for each required state and ignore stale priority-queue entries.

title: Minimum Edge Reversals From Source
description: Each directed edge `[u,v]` can be traversed from `u` to `v` at cost 0, or from `v` to `u` after reversing it at cost 1. For every vertex, find the minimum number of edge reversals needed for a route from `source`; return -1 when no route exists even after reversals. Input: `n`, `directedEdges`, `source`. Output: one minimum cost per vertex.
constraints: There are no duplicate directed edges
hints: Represent each edge as a transition whose cost matches the route rule.
Keep the best distance for each required state and ignore stale priority-queue entries.
